attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his newsletter, addressed rhetorically to Altman about OpenAI's search product.

semantics.note: Context ties the remark to OpenAI's search product. 'I don't think... at all!' is an emphatic statement of belief, not a graded probability, so it reads as an undated forecast. The proposition keeps his wording.

contract.note: Reading it as 'never profitable at product level' is the ordinary reading. Treating the ChatGPT search successor as in scope is reasonable. The contract correctly notes there is no accounting basis and no deadline.

evidence.note: OpenAI's own announcement showing SearchGPT was folded into ChatGPT search. It shows continuity of the product but gives no profit or loss figures.

reviews.rationale: This is an undated forecast that the search product will never be profitable. No deadline has passed, and the packet has no product-level accounts and no permanent shutdown, so no conclusive event exists. The only evidence shows product continuity. The claim cannot be scored yet.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his newsletter.

semantics.note: The proposition follows his words. But in context this is a polemical verdict in a call to 'atone'. 'Always unsustainable', 'stealing', 'vague' utility and 'overstated' ubiquity are evaluative characterisations with no measures, so this is rhetoric rather than a testable observation.

contract.note: To score this, the contract has to supply definitions of sustainability, theft, vagueness and overstatement, plus a way to combine four assertions. None of that comes from the speaker, so the result would turn on the evaluator's choices.

evidence.note: Adobe's statement about its own licensed training. It is a company disclosure, not an independent provenance finding.
Measured productivity gains in one 2020–21 customer-service deployment. That is a narrow application and cannot settle an industry-wide 'vague utility' verdict.
A 2024 survey finding infrequent use. It is consistent with limited routine adoption, but there is no identified publicity claim to compare it against.
A secondary account showing Firefly's provenance was complicated. It does not show that theft was necessary.
A mid-2024 investment analysis questioning returns. It leaves the payoff open and is not proof of unsustainability.

reviews.rationale: The sentence packs four evaluative judgments into a polemical conclusion, and none has a stated measure or threshold. Each could only be graded on definitions the speaker did not give, and the evidence only touches parts of it from different angles. It is too vague and value-laden to score fairly.

attribution.note: Zitron's own summary sentence in his newsletter.

semantics.note: A compound observation: about $19B of fiscal Q4 2024 capex, mostly on cloud and AI; stated plans to keep increasing spending; and limited money made by Microsoft and its users. The normalisation keeps all three parts.

contract.note: In context, reading 'expenses' as capex including finance leases fits. Reading 'not that much money' as limited returns relative to investment is ordinary. But no threshold or customer population is given, so the returns part depends on interpretation.

evidence.note: Microsoft's reported results: $19B capex including finance leases, nearly all cloud and AI related. This supports the spending element only. It is a company disclosure and does not isolate AI profit or customer returns.
A survey of leaders' perceived AI ROI across AI broadly. It neither measures Microsoft's generative AI customers' financial returns nor settles them.

reviews.rationale: The $19B cloud-and-AI capex figure is supported by Microsoft's reported results. The central claim that generative AI makes neither Microsoft nor its users much money is not settled: no product-level AI profit or representative customer return data is in the packet. The 'more than ever before' superlative is also unverified. Overall the claim is unresolved.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his newsletter.

semantics.note: 'In any case where this happens' refers to big tech absorbing OpenAI or Anthropic, Character.ai-style. The firm 'will eventually putter out' depends on that antecedent, and the normalisation keeps it.

contract.note: Reading 'putter out' as the residual entity ceasing substantive operations is ordinary. The contract rightly says that continued operation for a finite period cannot falsify 'eventually'.

evidence.note: OpenAI's structure page: the Foundation still controls OpenAI Group, so no big-tech absorption is shown.
Anthropic's 2026 IPO filing describes an independent PBC with trust governance, so no absorption is shown.

reviews.rationale: The forecast only applies if big tech absorbs OpenAI or Anthropic. The packet shows neither has happened: OpenAI is still under Foundation control and Anthropic has filed for an IPO as an independent company. With the antecedent unmet, there is no residual entity to track, so the conditional cannot be scored.
